title: The media's role in vaccine misinformation
screen_reason: The text file is not the paper named in the manifest. The manifest asks for 'The media's role in vaccine misinformation' (Scopus 2-s2.0-84929523850); the file contains a different document entirely: 'Coronavirus: vaccine misinformation and the role of social media', a King's College London Policy Institute / Ipsos MORI polling report dated Sunday 14 December 2020, contact Bobby Duffy, reporting an online i:omnibus survey of 2,244 UK residents aged 16-75 interviewed 20-24 November 2020. Different title, different year, different genre (a survey report, not a journal article), different authors (Duffy, Allington, Moxham-Hall, Smith, Beaver, Murkin, Meyer, Skinner, Rubin, Wessely, Strang). Protocol section 1 excludes a record when 'the text is not the paper named', so no estimate is recorded against this id. Note the two documents are easy to confuse: both are about vaccine misinformation and media, which is probably how the wrong PDF was attached.
missed_or_uncertain: Nothing was extracted because the id and the text do not match; the estimates below belong to the KCL/Ipsos MORI report that is in the file, NOT to the paper named in the manifest, and an adjudicator who decides to re-point this id at the report should code them from scratch. The document is eligible on its own terms and carries at least four RECALL rows: (1) '1 in 3 people (34%) in the UK say they've seen or heard messages discouraging the public from getting a coronavirus vaccine' (base 2,244 UK residents aged 16-75, 20-24 November 2020); (2) 'Overall, this amounts to 1 in 5 people (20%) in the UK saying they've seen such messages on Facebook' (a derived population figure the report states verbatim; the platform breakdown itself, Facebook 58%, friend/family 20%, Twitter 19%, Instagram 17%, YouTube 16%, television 15%, WhatsApp 13%, has base 771 - the subset who saw such messages - not the full sample); (3) 'Around 1 in 4 Britons (26%) say they've seen or heard Covid anti-vax messages on social media' (base 2,244), with the sharer breakdown (friend or family 42%, other 31%, news or lifestyle account 28%, celebrity or public figure 23%) on base 614; (4) the age and social-grade breakdowns of the 34% (16-24 49%, 25-34 44%, 35-44 34%, 45-54 24%, 55-75 25%; AB 45%, C1 30%, C2 33%, DE 25%) are demographic subgroups of the headline and would not normally be rows. The belief items (14% track and control, 15% profit motive, 9% DNA, 9% Bill Gates microchips, 7% infertility, 5% autism, and their by-platform breakdowns) are BELIEF in false claims, which section 1 excludes explicitly. The regulation-support items (67%, 67%, 55%, 54%) are attitudes, not exposure. Also worth flagging for whoever repairs the corpus: the report is grey literature (Ipsos MORI online omnibus, weighted, no response rate given), and the belief items use base 1,122 (a half-sample) while the exposure items use base 2,244.

rob.design: Not appraisable for the named paper, which is absent. The document actually present is an Ipsos MORI online i:omnibus survey of 2,244 UK adults aged 16-75 interviewed 20-24 November 2020, weighted to known offline population proportions for age within gender, government office region, working status, social grade and education; no response rate, no questionnaire appendix and no sampling-error estimate are given beyond a generic caveat, and the belief battery is asked of a 1,122-respondent half-sample.
